summary: An IFS report by Pascale Bourquin, Robert Joyce and David Sturrock, published 26 April 2021, projects how much inheritance UK household members born in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s will receive and how this affects living standards, inequality and social mobility. It finds inheritances are growing relative to incomes and will increasingly depend on parental wealth, and that anticipated inheritances lead the young to save less today. The research was funded by the Nuffield Foundation and the ESRC under the CPP grant.
one_line: IFS report projecting UK inheritances for 1960s-1980s-born generations and their effects on inequality, social mobility and saving.
key_facts: Inheritances have been growing as a share of national income in the UK since the 1970s, according to the report.
For those born in the 1960s, inheritances are projected to be worth 9% of household lifetime (non-inheritance) income; for those born in the 1980s, 16%.
Among the 1980s-born, the median lifetime inheritance for the bottom fifth by lifetime income is around £150,000, and for the top fifth around £390,000.
Among the 1980s-born, the median lifetime inheritance as a percentage of lifetime income is around 15% for the bottom fifth and 16% for the top fifth.

For those born in the 1960s, inheritances are projected to increase lifetime incomes by 2% on average for those with parents in the bottom fifth of the wealth distribution and by 17% for those with parents in the top fifth.
For those born in the 1980s, inheritances are projected to increase lifetime incomes by 5% for those with parents in the bottom wealth fifth and by 29% for those with parents in the top wealth fifth.
The percentage of individuals expecting to receive an inheritance rose from 72% of those born in the 1960s to 81% of those born in the 1980s.
An economic model projects that those born in the 1980s will on average hold 9%, or around £16,000, less wealth at age 45 because they anticipate a future inheritance.
For 1980s-born households, the bottom fifth by lifetime income spend 11% of their inheritance in advance of receiving it, whereas the top fifth spend 33% in advance.
The report concludes that policies successfully redistributing inheritances would have larger effects on inequality and social mobility for later-born generations.
The research is funded by the Nuffield Foundation and was released by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS).
The report was authored by Pascale Bourquin, Robert Joyce (Deputy Director) and David Sturrock (Senior Research Economist).
